summary.lead: Official summary (Congressional Research Service, Reported to Senate):

blocks.text: Consumer Labeling for Enhanced API Reporting and Legitimate Accountability for Base Entity Listings Act or the CLEAR LABELS Act
This bill requires drugs and active pharmaceutical ingredients made available in the U.S. market to be labeled with the names and locations of their manufacturers.

Specifically, a finished, packaged drug product must be labeled with the name and place of business of (1) the original manufacturer (or manufacturers) of each active pharmaceutical ingredient; (2) the original manufacturer of the finished drug product; and (3) the packer or distributor, if any. This information must be printed on the product label or made available electronically. Active pharmaceutical ingredients (which are generally sold to manufacturers and researchers, not consumers) must also be labeled with the name and place of business of their original manufacturers.
Under the bill, the original manufacturer is the establishment that conducts the majority of the significant phases of manufacturing to produce the ingredient or product.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has discretion to determine whether a violation of these requirements constitutes misbranding and to assess a civil fine. The FDA must consider certain factors in determining whether to assess a fine, including whether the violator was notified of their noncompliance and was provided an opportunity to correct the violation.
Finally, the FDA must coordinate with U.S. Customs and Border Protection to address any overlap between these requirements and existing requirements for imported drugs.
These provisions take effect five years after the bill is enacted.

The CLEAR LABELS Act would require drugs and their active ingredients sold in the U.S. to show where they were made. Drugs for consumers would need to be labeled with the name and location of the original manufacturer of each active ingredient, the original manufacturer of the finished product, and any packer or distributor involved. This information could be printed on the label or made available electronically. Active ingredients, which are usually sold to manufacturers and researchers rather than consumers, would also need to be labeled with the name and location of their original manufacturers.
Under the bill, the original manufacturer is the company that carries out most of the important steps in making the ingredient or product.

The Food and Drug Administration would decide whether a violation counts as misbranding and could impose a civil fine. In deciding whether to fine a company, the agency must consider certain factors, including whether the company was told about the violation and given a chance to fix it. The FDA would also work with U.S. Customs and Border Protection to handle any overlap with existing rules for imported drugs.
These requirements would take effect five years after the bill becomes law.
